items.readable_text:
Content:
Consider the matrix [MATH: [2|5; − 1|− 4]] How can we find its eigenvalues?

Content:
By definition, we need to find the value(s) of [MATH: \,\lambda\,] such that [MATH: \,A\mathbf{\color{blue}v} = \lambda \mathbf{\color{blue}v}\,] is true for some non-zero vector [MATH: \mathbf{\color{blue}v}.] Let's re-write this equation as follows:
[MATH: Av|= λv; Av − λv|= 0; Av − λIv|= 0; (A − λI)v|= 0]

Content:
The final equation above tells us that there should be at least one non-zero vector [MATH: \mathbf{\color{blue}v}] that lies in [MATH: \textrm{Null}(A-\lambda I)], the null space of the matrix [MATH: A-\lambda I.] As a result, the invertible matrix theorem tells us that the matrix [MATH: \, A-\lambda I \,] must be singular, meaning [MATH: \det(A-\lambda I) = 0.]

Content:
We've reduced the problem to finding the values of [MATH: \lambda] that satisfy the equation
[MATH: \det(A-\lambda I) = 0,]
which is called the characteristic equation of the matrix [MATH: A]. So, let's solve it!

Content:
First, we write down the matrix [MATH: A-\lambda I\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: A− λI|= [2|5; − 1|− 4]− λ[1|0; 0|1]; = [2− λ|5; − 1|− 4− λ]]

Content:
Then, we solve the characteristic equation [MATH: \det(A-\lambda I) = 0\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: det(A − λI)|= 0;|2 − λ|5; − 1|− 4 − λ||= 0; (2 − λ)(− 4 − λ) − 5 ⋅ (− 1)|= 0; − 8 − 2λ + 4λ + λ^{2} + 5|= 0; λ^{2} + 2λ − 3|= 0; (λ + 3)(λ − 1)|= 0]

Content:
Therefore, the eigenvalues of [MATH: A] are [MATH: \lambda=-3] and [MATH: \lambda=1.]

sections.normalized_html:
Let's start by writing the matrix [MATH: A - \lambda I\mathbin{:}] ﻿﻿[MATH: [10 − λ|3; 6|7 − λ]]

Now, let's find and solve the characteristic equation [MATH: \det(A-\lambda I) = 0\mathbin{:}] [MATH: det(A − λI)|= 0;|10 − λ|3; 6|7 − λ||= 0; (10 − λ)(7 − λ) − 3 ⋅ 6|= 0; 70 − 7λ − 10λ + λ^{2} − 18|= 0; λ^{2} − 17λ + 52|= 0]

Using the quadratic formula, we obtain

[MATH: λ|= (17 ± sqrt((− 17)^{2} − 4 ⋅ 1 ⋅ 52))/(2 ⋅ 1); = (17 ± sqrt(81))/(2); = (17 ± 9)/(2); = 13, 4.]

Therefore, the eigenvalues are [MATH: \lambda=13] and [MATH: \lambda=4.]

items.title: Calculating the Eigenvalues of a Triangular/Diagonal Matrix

sections.normalized_html: Find all real eigenvalues of the matrix [MATH: [3|0; 9|− 2sqrt(3)]]
sections.readable_text: Find all real eigenvalues of the matrix [MATH: [3|0; 9|− 2sqrt(3)]]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Let's start by writing the matrix [MATH: A - \lambda I \mathbin{:}] ﻿﻿﻿[MATH: [3 − λ|0; 9|− 2sqrt(3) − λ]]

Now, let's find and solve the characteristic equation [MATH: \det (A - \lambda I) = 0\mathbin{:}] [MATH: det(A − λI)|= 0;|3 − λ|0; 9|− 2sqrt(3) − λ||= 0; (3 − λ)(− 2sqrt(3) − λ) − 9 ⋅ 0|= 0; (λ − 3)(λ + 2sqrt(3))|= 0]

So, we get the eigenvalues [MATH: \lambda={\color{red}3}] and [MATH: \lambda={\color{blue}-2\sqrt{3}}.]

If we look again at the matrix [MATH: [3|0; 9|− 2sqrt(3)]] we see that the eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal. This is true in general: the eigenvalues of a triangular or diagonal matrix are always given by the entries on the main diagonal!

Watch out! For a general matrix (which is neither triangular nor diagonal), this might not be the case!

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Consider the matrix [MATH: [2|5; − 1|− 4]] How can we find its eigenvalues?

Content:
By definition, we need to find the value(s) of [MATH: \,\lambda\,] such that [MATH: \,A\mathbf{\color{blue}v} = \lambda \mathbf{\color{blue}v}\,] is true for some non-zero vector [MATH: \mathbf{\color{blue}v}.] Let's re-write this equation as follows:
[MATH: Av|= λv; Av − λv|= 0; Av − λIv|= 0; (A − λI)v|= 0]

Content:
The final equation above tells us that there should be at least one non-zero vector [MATH: \mathbf{\color{blue}v}] that lies in [MATH: \textrm{Null}(A-\lambda I)], the null space of the matrix [MATH: A-\lambda I.] As a result, the invertible matrix theorem tells us that the matrix [MATH: \, A-\lambda I \,] must be singular, meaning [MATH: \det(A-\lambda I) = 0.]

Content:
We've reduced the problem to finding the values of [MATH: \lambda] that satisfy the equation
[MATH: \det(A-\lambda I) = 0,]
which is called the characteristic equation of the matrix [MATH: A]. So, let's solve it!

Content:
First, we write down the matrix [MATH: A-\lambda I\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: A− λI|= [2|5; − 1|− 4]− λ[1|0; 0|1]; = [2− λ|5; − 1|− 4− λ]]

Content:
Then, we solve the characteristic equation [MATH: \det(A-\lambda I) = 0\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: det(A − λI)|= 0;|2 − λ|5; − 1|− 4 − λ||= 0; (2 − λ)(− 4 − λ) − 5 ⋅ (− 1)|= 0; − 8 − 2λ + 4λ + λ^{2} + 5|= 0; λ^{2} + 2λ − 3|= 0; (λ + 3)(λ − 1)|= 0]

Content:
Therefore, the eigenvalues of [MATH: A] are [MATH: \lambda=-3] and [MATH: \lambda=1.]

---

Item 5 — Tutorial: The Number of Real Eigenvalues of a 2x2 Matrix

Content:
The characteristic equation of any [MATH: 2 \!\times\! 2] matrix [MATH: A] is always a quadratic equation, which implies that [MATH: A] has at most [MATH: 2] eigenvalues. Here are the all possible cases:

Content:
- Two distinct real eigenvalues
- One repeated real eigenvalue (or, equivalently, two real eigenvalues that are the same)
- No real eigenvalues (or, equivalently, two complex eigenvalues)

Item 6 — Example: Computing the Eigenvalues of a Matrix With Two Distinct Eigenvalues

Example Prompt:
Find all real eigenvalues of the matrix [MATH: [10|3; 6|7]]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let's start by writing the matrix [MATH: A - \lambda I\mathbin{:}]
﻿﻿[MATH: [10 − λ|3; 6|7 − λ]]

Now, let's find and solve the characteristic equation [MATH: \det(A-\lambda I) = 0\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: det(A − λI)|= 0;|10 − λ|3; 6|7 − λ||= 0; (10 − λ)(7 − λ) − 3 ⋅ 6|= 0; 70 − 7λ − 10λ + λ^{2} − 18|= 0; λ^{2} − 17λ + 52|= 0]

Using the quadratic formula, we obtain

[MATH: λ|= (17 ± sqrt((− 17)^{2} − 4 ⋅ 1 ⋅ 52))/(2 ⋅ 1); = (17 ± sqrt(81))/(2); = (17 ± 9)/(2); = 13, 4.]

Therefore, the eigenvalues are [MATH: \lambda=13] and [MATH: \lambda=4.]

Item 9 — Example: Computing the Eigenvalues of a Matrix With At Most One Distinct Eigenvalue

Example Prompt:
Find all real eigenvalues of the matrix
[MATH: [4|0; 0|4]]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let's start by writing the matrix [MATH: B-\lambda I\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: [4 − λ|0; 0|4 − λ]]

Now, let's find and solve the characteristic equation [MATH: \det(B-\lambda I) = 0\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: det(B − λI)|= 0;|4 − λ|0; 0|4 − λ||= 0; (4 − λ)(4 − λ) − 0 ⋅ 0|= 0; (λ − 4)^{2}|= 0]

Therefore, the matrix [MATH: B] has only one eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda=4,] which is a double root of the characteristic equation.

Note: We also say that [MATH: \lambda=4] has an algebraic multiplicity of [MATH: 2.]

Item 12 — Example: Calculating the Eigenvalues of a Triangular/Diagonal Matrix

Example Prompt:
Find all real eigenvalues of the matrix [MATH: [3|0; 9|− 2sqrt(3)]]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let's start by writing the matrix [MATH: A - \lambda I \mathbin{:}]
﻿﻿﻿[MATH: [3 − λ|0; 9|− 2sqrt(3) − λ]]

Now, let's find and solve the characteristic equation [MATH: \det (A - \lambda I) = 0\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: det(A − λI)|= 0;|3 − λ|0; 9|− 2sqrt(3) − λ||= 0; (3 − λ)(− 2sqrt(3) − λ) − 9 ⋅ 0|= 0; (λ − 3)(λ + 2sqrt(3))|= 0]

So, we get the eigenvalues [MATH: \lambda={\color{red}3}] and [MATH: \lambda={\color{blue}-2\sqrt{3}}.]

If we look again at the matrix [MATH: [3|0; 9|− 2sqrt(3)]]
we see that the eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal. This is true in general: the eigenvalues of a triangular or diagonal matrix are always given by the entries on the main diagonal!

Watch out! For a general matrix (which is neither triangular nor diagonal), this might not be the case!
